channel.title: Top Scams & Frauds on Cybervattam
channel.description: Recent content in Top Scams & Frauds on Cybervattam

item.title: AI-Powered Scams
item.description:
Artificial intelligence can make scam emails, messages, calls, and videos look or sound convincing. Criminals may imitate a trusted person, manager, supplier, organisation, or family member using generated text, cloned voices, or deepfake video.

Warning signs

  • The request is urgent, unusual, emotional, or asks you to bypass normal processes.
  • A familiar person asks for money, credentials, or confidential information through a new channel.
  • A voice or video seems slightly unnatural, or the details do not match the usual context.

Stay safe

  • Pause before acting on urgent or emotional requests.
  • Verify the request independently using a known phone number or established contact method.
  • Use multi-factor authentication and keep devices, applications, and security software updated.
  • Never share passwords, PINs, one-time codes, or sensitive information merely because a message sounds authentic.

item.title: Bank Impersonation Scams
item.description:
A bank impersonation scam occurs when a criminal contacts you while pretending to be your bank. The aim is usually to steal login details, card information, one-time codes, or money.

How it works

A caller, text, or email may claim that your account has been compromised and direct you to a fake website, chat, or remote-access tool. You may be told to move money to a supposedly safe account.

item.title: Charity Scams
item.description:
Charity scams use fake charities, copied identities, or false fundraising campaigns to collect donations. They often appear during disasters, emergencies, or major news events.

Warning signs

  • An unsolicited request by phone, email, text, social media, or door-to-door contact.
  • Pressure to donate immediately or guilt-based emotional appeals.
  • Requests for cash, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or direct transfer.
  • Little information about the charity, its purpose, or how donations are used.

Stay safe

  • Verify the organisation through the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission register.
  • Visit the charity or fundraising platform directly instead of following an unsolicited link.
  • Use a secure payment method with transaction protections.
  • Keep receipts and report suspicious campaigns to the relevant authorities.

item.title: Credit Card Fraud
item.description:
Credit card fraud occurs when card details are used without the cardholder’s permission. Details may be stolen through phishing, unsafe websites, malware, skimming, data breaches, or social engineering.

Warning signs

  • Transactions you do not recognise.
  • Unexpected verification messages or replacement-card notices.
  • Requests for the card number, expiry date, security code, PIN, or one-time code.

Stay safe

  • Keep card details and one-time codes confidential.
  • Use secure websites and avoid entering details after following an unsolicited link.
  • Enable transaction alerts, review statements, and set sensible card limits.
  • Contact your card provider immediately to block or cancel a card when fraud is suspected.

item.title: Business Email Compromise
item.description:
Business email compromise occurs when criminals hack or spoof an email account to impersonate an executive, colleague, supplier, accountant, or lawyer. They request payments, confidential information, or changes to payment details.

Common scenarios

  • An executive asks for an urgent transfer or gift cards.
  • A supplier invoice is intercepted and its account details are changed.
  • A familiar contact requests a new bank account for future payments.
  • A property deposit or other high-value payment is redirected.

Stay safe

  • Verify payment requests and account changes by calling a known number.
  • Use approval procedures requiring more than one person for high-value payments.
  • Enable multi-factor authentication and keep software updated.
  • Check sender domains, signatures, tone, attachments, and payment details for small changes.

item.title: Email Scams
item.description:
An email scam is a message designed to make you click a malicious link, open an unsafe attachment, disclose information, or send money. Phishing is a common form of email scam.

Warning signs

  • Unexpected messages that create urgency or fear.
  • Links, attachments, or requests for credentials and payment details.
  • Sender addresses, names, or writing styles that do not match the claimed organisation.
  • Unexpected password-reset notices or messages sent from your account.

Stay safe

  • Do not click unexpected links or open unrequested attachments.
  • Verify requests using contact details found independently.
  • Use a unique password, multi-factor authentication, spam filtering, and current software.
  • If your account is compromised, change passwords, sign out other sessions, update recovery details, and scan your devices.

item.title: Gambling Scams
item.description:
Gambling scams use fake online betting, casino, or slot-style websites and apps. They may promise free spins, large bonuses, or guaranteed winnings but are designed to collect money and personal details.

Warning signs

  • The operator cannot be verified on the Australian Communications and Media Authority register.
  • Payment is requested by direct transfer, PayID, cryptocurrency, or card only.
  • Withdrawals are delayed, blocked, or require extra fees.
  • The offer is promoted through social media with unrealistic winning claims.

Stay safe

  • Verify that the operator is licensed before registering or paying.
  • Do not share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  • Stop using a suspicious app, change related passwords, and report the activity to your bank and relevant authorities.

item.title: Identity Theft and Identity Fraud
item.description:
Identity theft occurs when someone obtains personal information and uses it to impersonate you. Criminals may use names, addresses, dates of birth, licence or passport details, health identifiers, and account information to open accounts or commit fraud.

Warning signs

  • Transactions, bills, credit enquiries, or accounts you do not recognise.
  • Missing statements, changed contact details, or unexpected password resets.
  • Alerts about unfamiliar logins or repeated authentication attempts.
  • Unexpected tax, benefits, rebate, or credit notifications.

Stay safe

  • Use strong unique passwords and multi-factor authentication.
  • Monitor account activity and obtain your credit report regularly.
  • Limit personal information shared publicly and securely destroy sensitive documents.
  • Keep devices updated and report suspicious activity quickly.

If your identity may be compromised, contact affected organisations, change passwords and PINs, consider a credit-report ban, and seek support from IDCARE.

item.title: Investment Scams
item.description:
Investment scams promote fake or non-existent investments, often promising unusually high returns with little or no risk. Contact may begin through a call, social media, email, or text message.

Warning signs

  • An unsolicited financial expert offers rapid wealth or guaranteed returns.
  • Pressure to invest quickly or keep the opportunity secret.
  • No verifiable licence, registration, office, or investment history.
  • Fake websites, statements, celebrity endorsements, or professional-looking platforms.

Stay safe

  • Verify advisers and businesses through official Australian Securities and Investments Commission registers.
  • Do not accept unsolicited investment advice through social media.
  • Research independently, seek advice from a registered professional, and take time to decide.
  • Monitor your accounts and never transfer money solely because a website shows profits.

item.title: Job Scams
item.description:
Job scams advertise or offer employment that promises high pay for little effort. Criminals may seek recruitment fees, personal information, access to accounts, or use of your account to move money.

Warning signs

  • You are offered a job you did not apply for or hired before an interview.
  • You must pay an onboarding fee or buy products or equipment.
  • You are asked to use your personal bank or cryptocurrency account for company funds.
  • The employer has no verifiable address or the offer is not addressed to you.

Stay safe

  • Research the employer through independently verified contact details.
  • Never pay to obtain a job or transfer funds through your personal account.
  • Treat social-media side-hustles and encrypted-message offers with caution.
  • Report suspicious listings to the platform where they appeared.

item.title: Money Mule Scams
item.description:
A money mule is a person used to receive, transfer, or withdraw money obtained through crime. Recruitment may happen through fake jobs, romance scams, social media, or stolen identity details.

Warning signs

  • You are offered easy money for moving funds through your account.
  • An online romantic contact asks you to hold or transfer money.
  • A job requires your account to receive and forward payments.
  • Someone sends money “by mistake” and asks you to forward it elsewhere.

Stay safe

  • Do not allow online contacts or unknown employers to use your account.
  • Verify payment requests through an independent channel.
  • Never share passwords, PINs, one-time codes, or identity documents.
  • Contact your bank immediately if suspicious funds enter your account, and do not move them.

item.title: Online Sales Scams
item.description:
Online sales scams target buyers and sellers on fake stores and marketplaces. A fake seller may take payment without sending goods; a fake buyer may send a false payment notice or claim to have overpaid.

Warning signs

  • The price is far below comparable listings.
  • A seller refuses reasonable questions or has a new, incomplete profile.
  • A buyer asks you to upgrade an account or refund an overpayment.
  • A website lacks business details, contact information, privacy terms, or secure payment options.

Stay safe

  • Use trusted platforms and keep communications within the platform.
  • Confirm money is in your account; do not rely on screenshots or emailed receipts.
  • Check business details and research unfamiliar sellers.
  • Do not refund alleged overpayments until the original payment has cleared.

item.title: Phishing
item.description:
Phishing uses email, text messages, social media, or phone calls to impersonate a trusted source and steal information or money. Text phishing is called smishing, and phone phishing is called vishing.

Warning signs

  • A link or attachment in an unexpected message.
  • Urgency, threats, or a claim that you will lose money or face penalties.
  • Generic greetings, misspelled domains, unusual characters, or requests for credentials.
  • A prize or competition requiring personal or financial details.

Stay safe

  • Do not use links supplied in unexpected messages; visit the organisation’s site directly.
  • Never share passwords, card details, PINs, or one-time codes in response to a message or call.
  • Enable multi-factor authentication and keep software updated.
  • Avoid sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi and log out of important sessions when finished.

item.title: Phone Porting and SIM Swap Scams
item.description:
A phone porting or SIM swap scam transfers your mobile number to a SIM or eSIM controlled by a criminal. The criminal can receive calls, text messages, and SMS security codes used to access accounts.

Warning signs

  • Your phone unexpectedly displays SOS or No service without an outage.
  • You receive an unexpected notification about a new SIM or provider.
  • You see unfamiliar logins or transactions and cannot receive security codes.

Stay safe

  • Set a security PIN with your telecommunications provider.
  • Use authenticator apps or passkeys instead of SMS authentication where possible.
  • Protect personal details, use unique passwords, and shred documents containing identity information.
  • Contact your provider immediately if service stops unexpectedly, then contact your bank about suspicious activity.

item.title: Quishing and QR Code Scams
item.description:
Quishing is phishing delivered through a QR code. A fraudulent code may open a fake login page, trigger an unsafe download, or send you to a payment site controlled by a criminal.

Warning signs

  • The code arrives unexpectedly or is paired with urgency or threats.
  • It is pasted over a legitimate code in a public place.
  • The destination address looks unusual or asks for sensitive details.

Stay safe

  • Preview and inspect the web address after scanning before continuing.
  • Type addresses manually for sensitive logins and payments.
  • Download apps from official app stores rather than QR links.
  • Keep devices updated, use multi-factor authentication, and avoid scanning unknown codes.

item.title: Ransomware
item.description:
Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts files or blocks access to a device and demands payment. Criminals may also steal data and threaten to publish it.

How it spreads

  • Suspicious links or attachments.
  • Malicious websites or untrusted applications.
  • Infected USB devices.
  • Compromised accounts or online sessions.

Signs and protection

  • Locked files, unfamiliar extensions, disabled security tools, or a ransom note are warning signs.
  • Keep software updated, use security protection, enable multi-factor authentication, restrict permissions, and back up important data.
  • If attacked, record the details, disconnect the device and other devices from the network, and change important passwords from a clean device. Do not assume payment guarantees recovery.

item.title: Remote Access Scams
item.description:
A remote access scam tricks you into installing software or granting control of your computer or phone. The criminal may steal information, install malware, or access online banking.

Warning signs

  • An unexpected caller or pop-up claims your device has a virus.
  • Pressure to act immediately or pay with gift cards or unusual methods.
  • A request to install remote-control software or log in to your bank.
  • The cursor, settings, files, or performance change unexpectedly.

Stay safe

  • Never grant access to an unknown person who contacts you unexpectedly.
  • Initiate support yourself through a verified official channel.
  • Keep operating systems, security software, and applications updated.
  • If access was granted, disconnect from the internet, scan the device, change sensitive passwords from another device, and contact your bank.

item.title: Scam Calls and Spam Calls
item.description:
A scam call uses a phone conversation to impersonate a trusted organisation or person and obtain information or money. Spam calls are unwanted marketing, but scam calls may include deception, threats, or requests for payment.

Warning signs

  • An unknown, overseas, hidden, or unexpected number.
  • Requests for passwords, banking details, payments, or remote access.
  • Threats of arrest, fines, service disconnection, or other consequences.
  • An offer of guaranteed investment returns or an unusually cheap service.

Stay safe

  • Let unknown calls go to voicemail and hang up when a request seems suspicious.
  • Call the organisation back using a trusted number, not one supplied by the caller.
  • Enable phone spam filtering and block or report suspicious numbers.
  • Keep personal contact details private and never share PINs or passwords by phone.

item.title: Scam Text Messages
item.description:
Scam text messages, also called smishing, use SMS to impersonate an organisation or family member. They commonly contain a link or phone number designed to steal information, install malware, or obtain payment.

Common scenarios

  • A fake account alert or refund.
  • An unpaid toll or parcel redirection request.
  • A message from a supposed child using a new number.

Stay safe

  • Pause and do not click links or call numbers in unexpected texts.
  • Verify the request using a known number or official app.
  • Never send personal or banking information by text.
  • Block and report the sender, enable spam filtering, and contact your bank immediately if details were shared.

item.title: Social Media Scams
item.description:
Social media scams use profiles, posts, messages, advertisements, and marketplaces to obtain money or personal information.

Common forms

  • Fake profiles of friends, relatives, celebrities, charities, or businesses.
  • Marketplace listings, fake prizes, and investment offers.
  • Fake employment offers and malicious links on professional networks.

Stay safe

  • Keep profiles private and limit public personal details such as location, birth date, and phone number.
  • Enable multi-factor authentication and use unique passwords.
  • Verify unexpected contacts; reverse-search profile images when appropriate.
  • Never send money, sensitive information, or intimate media to someone known only online.

item.title: Spoof Calls and Fake Caller IDs
item.description:
Caller ID spoofing falsifies the number or name displayed on your phone so a criminal appears to be a trusted person or organisation. The caller may then seek money or personal information.

Warning signs

  • An unexpected call appears to come from a familiar organisation.
  • The caller creates urgency, threatens consequences, or asks for sensitive details.
  • The caller cannot provide a reference you can verify independently.

Stay safe

  • Do not trust caller ID as proof of identity.
  • Let unexpected calls go to voicemail or hang up when anything feels wrong.
  • Call back using an official number you already know.
  • Enable built-in call filtering or a reputable screening service and report suspicious calls.

item.title: Unexpected Money and Inheritance Scams
item.description:
Unexpected-money scams claim that you have won a prize, inherited money, or are owed a payment. The criminal asks for personal details, an upfront fee, or access to an account before releasing the supposed funds.

Common scenarios

  • Lottery or competition prize claims.
  • An inheritance from an unknown relative.
  • A tax refund or other unexpected payment.

Warning signs and protection

  • Unexpected contact, time pressure, requests for passwords, or a fee to claim money.
  • Do not click links or share PINs, passwords, banking details, or one-time codes.
  • Verify claims through an independently sourced official contact.
  • Legitimate winnings or refunds do not require you to pay an upfront fee to receive them.
